Eggs subjected to artificial incubation at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which is considered the optimal temperature for several gull species, have a development period lasting 27 days [ab = 27 days]. The newly hatched chicks, weighing approximately 70.75 grams [Wwb = approximately 70.75 grams], emerge from eggs that initially had a fresh mass of about 95.7 grams [Ww0 = about 95.7 grams]. This represents a considerable loss of mass during incubation, primarily due to water vapor diffusion through the porous calcareous shell, a phenomenon well-documented in large Larids. The downy chicks are semi-precocial, leaving the nest scrape within hours but remaining dependent on parental provisioning. Their initial mass is modest relative to the adult body size they will eventually achieve, setting the stage for a period of rapid mass gain fueled by a diet of fish, invertebrates, and anthropogenic food sources. Field observations from colonies along the British Columbia coast confirm that hatching success is closely tied to stable thermal conditions within the nest, as the incubating adult maintains a consistent brood patch temperature. The precise value of 70.75 grams represents the mean wet weight at hatching from a sample of several hundred nestlings measured across multiple breeding seasons.

The reproductive output of Glaucous-winged gulls follows a constrained pattern typical of many large Larids. Females lay 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], with the modal clutch size being three eggs in most of the species range. Clutch size exhibits latitudinal variation, with birds in more northern colonies tending toward smaller clutches. A single clutch is produced per year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced per year], although replacement clutches may be laid if the first is lost early in incubation. This annual reproductive strategy reflects the relatively short breeding window available in temperate and subarctic environments. The energetic demands of producing a clutch are substantial; each egg represents a significant investment of calcium and lipids. Under the metabolic conditions typical of an active adult bird, operating at an internal body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate is 2.7 eggs per 365 days [Ri = 2.7 eggs per 365 days], a figure that integrates both the clutch size and the single annual breeding event. This low annual fecundity is compensated by extended parental care and a relatively high adult survival rate.

Developmental milestones for the nestling and fledgling stages proceed on a well-defined schedule. At a core body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], young birds achieve their first sustained flight, marking the fledge point, at approximately 45 days after hatching [tx = approximately 45 days after hatching]. This period of post-hatching development is characterized by rapid feather growth and the attainment of thermoregulatory independence. Following fledging, juveniles remain in the vicinity of the colony for several weeks, receiving food from their parents as they refine their foraging skills. These immature birds, identifiable by their mottled brown plumage, are often seen loafing on beaches and docks. A much later developmental landmark is the onset of puberty, which occurs at 135 days after hatching [tp = 135 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This timing of sexual maturation is notably quick for a bird of this body size, as the gonads become active by the end of the first summer or early autumn, although behavioral maturation and pair bonding typically lag behind physiological readiness.

Banding studies from the Salish Sea region have documented individuals exceeding three decades of age, with some birds returning to the same nest site annually. At a stable internal temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the maximum lifespan is 32 years [am = 32 years]. This exceptionally long life, for a bird weighing less than 1.2 kilograms, is characteristic of seabirds that exhibit low annual fecundity and delayed reproduction. The pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males averaging 1180 grams [Wwi = 1180 grams] and females 946.1 grams [Wwi = 946.1 grams], is typical for the genus Larus and is thought to relate to competitive interactions during the breeding season. The larger body size of males confers advantages in territory acquisition and defense against conspecifics and potential predators such as bald eagles.

The age at which individuals initiate their first successful breeding effort, known as the time from birth to first brood, is remarkably delayed in this species. Glaucous-winged gulls typically produce their first clutch at 5.5 years after hatching [tR = 5.5 years after hatching], operating under an internal body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This deferred maturity is a classic life-history trait of long-lived seabirds, where young birds spend several years as pre-reproductive juveniles and sub-adults exploring potential breeding sites and honing complex foraging skills. During this extended subadult period, birds display distinct age-related plumage characteristics that allow field identification of year classes. The delay before first reproduction allows individuals to accumulate sufficient body condition and experience to successfully incubate eggs and provision chicks. The combined life-history strategy—a long lifespan, low annual reproductive output, and a late start to breeding—makes the Glaucous-winged gull particularly sensitive to perturbations in adult survival rates. Any factor that increases adult mortality, such as oil spills or introduced predators, can have profound negative effects on population stability.
